chunk_findings.detail: The new predicate treats “not `@runtime_checkable`” as “several adapters.” That is not the multi-adapter rule the bug describes. Given Optimizer (several adapters in a Registry, `name` omitted so the Protocol can stay `@runtime_checkable`, `_is_runtime_protocol` true), `multi` is false and the else branch still asserts `"name" not in cls.__annotations__`. The test stays green and still forces that family to omit `name`. The opposite input fails wrongly too: a one-adapter Protocol with no `@runtime_checkable` (`_is_runtime_protocol` false or missing, so `getattr` yields false) is classified multi and required to declare `name`, which the same test says invites a one-entry registry. No marker or registry size is consulted, so the Forge literal is gone but the bug is not closed.

data.probe: Optimizer MUST omit name from its Protocol for a real, test-independent reason: tests/test_adapter_optimizer.py:65-66 assert isinstance(O.GreedyV1(), Optimizer) and isinstance(FakeOptimizer(), Optimizer), which require @runtime_checkable; declaring name: str (data) on a runtime Protocol makes isinstance raise TypeError ("Instance and class checks can only be used with @runtime_checkable protocols"). So the fix does NOT force Optimizer to omit name -- Optimizer omits it so its faked adapters stay runtime-verifiable, and name lives on the adapter (GreedyV1.name="greedy-v1"). The derived rule name-in-port <=> not @runtime_checkable is exact, not a listing: the sole data member a port may hold on the declaration-only model is name (the registry key), so a non-runtime port is one that declares name. A second registry family that wants name in its port (no fake to verify) is free to do so now. The Forge literal is gone AND the rule is read off the runtime_checkable marker.

chunk_findings.detail: `take_over = _take_over(item_id, agent)` is assigned only on the still-held / grace-period path, immediately before that path's `raise LeaseError`. The swept-empty and unswept expired refusals (the `expired_at` messages that now interpolate `{take_over}`) are other branches and do not run that assignment. Claiming an item whose lease already has `expired_at` set — the case the bug is about, e.g. after `ddflow recover --apply` on an empty tree, or an unswept crash — hits `UnboundLocalError` instead of a refusal, so neither `--force` nor `--approval request` is ever named.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/claim.py:_take_over

chunk_findings.detail: The `force` parameter text still says a person may retry with `force` only after `ddflow_recover` reported that the tree holds nothing. `recovery.md` says either way a person takes the item back with `ddflow claim <item> --force`, and the unswept expired `LeaseError` tells a person to `claim --force` when the tree may still hold work. A person with a tree that holds finished work is told three incompatible things about the same flag, which is the contradiction Bbb8c158254 required the three texts to stop telling.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle/navigate.py:force help

chunk_findings.detail: The person regression is set up with `_crashed_with_work(repo)` and no `recover(apply=True)`, so the expired lease is still unswept and the tree still holds work, but the assertions only require `ddflow claim T1 --force` and forbid `--approval request`. They never require `ddflow recover --item T1`. A refusal that tells a person only to `ddflow claim T1 --force` therefore passes, which is the contradiction this bug names: `--force` on a tree that has not been swept and still holds work, instead of recover-then-force.
